Finding.title: Client-controlled cookie is deserialized with pickle

codeEvidence.label: Cookie value is deserialized directly
codeEvidence.explanation: A browser-controlled cookie is base64-decoded and passed to pickle.loads without authentication, integrity verification, or a safe data parser.

codeEvidence.label: Application sets the same cookie as pickle data
codeEvidence.explanation: The server-created cookie format is pickle data, but the later read path trusts client-supplied cookie bytes as valid pickle.

rootCause.summary: The application uses Python pickle as a client-side cookie serialization format and deserializes the cookie on the server without authenticity protection.

validation.summary: Static validation confirmed an unauthenticated GET request can supply the value cookie and reach pickle.loads. No runtime payload execution was performed.
validation.counterevidence: The value is base64-encoded when the app sets it, but base64 is reversible and does not provide integrity or authenticity.

dataflow.summary: HTTP Cookie value -> b64decode -> pickle.loads -> Python deserialization semantics in the Flask process.

reachability.summary: /cookie is registered for GET and POST and the cookie read path executes on non-POST requests when the cookie is present.

prerequisites: The attacker can set a value cookie in their request.

Finding.impact: A crafted pickle stream may execute code or instantiate attacker-chosen objects in the application process, leading to process compromise or denial of service.
Finding.remediation: Do not deserialize pickle data from clients. Store only simple signed JSON or server-side session identifiers, and protect client-side state with an authenticated integrity mechanism.

Finding.title: DNS lookup route concatenates form input into an OS command

codeEvidence.label: Command helper invokes os.popen
codeEvidence.explanation: The helper passes a command string to os.popen, which executes it through the operating-system command processor.

codeEvidence.label: Address form value is concatenated into command string
codeEvidence.code:
if request.method == 'POST': address = request.form['address'] return """ """ + "Result:\n
\n" + (rp("nslookup " + address).replace('\n', '\n
') if address else "") + """
codeEvidence.explanation: The address field flows into the command string without validation, escaping, or argument-vector separation.

rootCause.summary: Untrusted form data is concatenated into a shell command and executed through os.popen.

validation.summary: Static validation confirmed a direct form-input-to-command path. No command payload was executed.
validation.counterevidence: No allowlist, subprocess argument list, or shell-disabled execution path is present.

dataflow.summary: POST /lookup address -> string concatenation into nslookup command -> rp() -> os.popen.

reachability.summary: /lookup accepts unauthenticated GET and POST requests.

prerequisites: The runtime shell honors injected command syntax.

Finding.impact: An attacker can potentially execute arbitrary host commands with the Flask process privileges, exposing local files, environment data, database credentials, or availability.
Finding.remediation: Avoid shell command construction. Use a DNS resolver library or invoke subprocess with a fixed executable and validated argument list, with shell disabled.

Finding.title: Expression evaluation route executes user input with eval

codeEvidence.label: Form expression is evaluated as Python code
codeEvidence.code:
if request.method == 'POST': expression = request.form['expression'] return """ """ + "Result: " + (str(eval(expression)).replace('\n', '\n
') if expression else "") + """
codeEvidence.explanation: The expression field is evaluated directly with Python eval in the application process.

rootCause.summary: The route treats untrusted HTTP input as executable Python expression text.

validation.summary: Static validation confirmed direct use of eval on request.form data. No runtime expression was submitted.
validation.counterevidence: No restricted globals, sandbox, parser, or expression allowlist is supplied to eval.

dataflow.summary: POST /evaluate expression -> eval(expression) -> Python interpreter execution context.

reachability.summary: /evaluate accepts unauthenticated GET and POST requests.

Finding.impact: Attacker-controlled Python expression execution can compromise the Flask process, read in-memory configuration/secrets, access files, or disrupt service.
Finding.remediation: Remove eval for untrusted input. Implement a safe expression parser or a strict allowlist of supported operations with no access to Python objects or globals.

Finding.title: XML parser enables DTD loading and network access for user-supplied XML

codeEvidence.label: XML parser allows network access and DTD loading
codeEvidence.code:
if request.method == 'POST':
        xml = request.form['xml']
        parser = etree.XMLParser(no_network=False, dtd_validation=False, load_dtd=True, huge_tree=True)
        #try:
        doc = etree.fromstring(xml.encode(), parser)
        parsed_xml = etree.tostring(doc).decode('utf8')
codeEvidence.explanation: The route parses attacker-controlled XML with DTD loading enabled and network access not disabled.

rootCause.summary: Untrusted XML is parsed with lxml options that permit DTD processing and network access.

validation.summary: Static validation confirmed unsafe parser configuration and direct parsing of request data. Entity resolution was not tested dynamically.
validation.counterevidence: The route escapes serialized output before HTML rendering, but that does not prevent parser-side file or network access.

reachability.summary: /xml accepts unauthenticated GET and POST requests.

prerequisites: The lxml/libxml2 runtime resolves the submitted external entity or DTD construct.
The process can access useful local files or network destinations.

Finding.impact: An attacker may be able to read process-accessible files, induce server-side network requests, or trigger parser resource exhaustion depending on runtime behavior.
Finding.remediation: Disable DTD and external entity processing for untrusted XML. Use a hardened XML parser configuration with network access disabled and entity resolution blocked.

Finding.title: Config endpoint decrypts attacker-controlled ciphertext and returns padding errors

codeEvidence.label: AES-CBC decrypt returns padding-specific errors
codeEvidence.explanation: The decrypt path uses CBC mode and raises distinguishable padding exceptions.

codeEvidence.label: Chosen ciphertext is decrypted and exception text is returned
codeEvidence.explanation: The key query parameter is attacker-controlled ciphertext and decryption errors are returned in the HTTP response.

rootCause.summary: The config lookup design exposes unauthenticated AES-CBC decryption of chosen ciphertext and leaks exception text.

validation.summary: Static validation confirmed attacker-controlled ciphertext reaches decrypt() and padding errors are returned. No iterative oracle exploitation was performed.
validation.counterevidence: The endpoint restricts normal links to app_* config keys, but that restriction is applied before attacker-chosen key values are decrypted.

dataflow.summary: GET /config key -> unhexlify -> AES-CBC decrypt -> unpad -> exception text returned.

reachability.summary: /config is a GET route and does not require authentication.

prerequisites: The attacker can submit chosen key parameter values.
The response differences are observable across ciphertext attempts.

Finding.impact: A padding oracle can allow attackers to recover or forge encrypted config-key values, potentially exposing non-viewable CONFIG entries such as secret-bearing values.
Finding.remediation: Use authenticated encryption or add a message authentication check before decryption. Do not return raw cryptographic exception details to clients.

Finding.title: Greeting route renders user input as Jinja template source

codeEvidence.label: User name is interpolated into template before rendering
codeEvidence.code:
if request.method == 'POST': name = '
Hello %s!

' %(request.form['name']) ... template = """ ... %s ... """ %(name) return render_template_string(template)
codeEvidence.explanation: The name field is inserted into the template source and then rendered by Jinja, rather than being passed as an escaped template variable.

rootCause.summary: The route constructs a Jinja template string with untrusted data before calling render_template_string.

validation.summary: Static validation confirmed request.form['name'] becomes template source. No template payload was executed.
validation.counterevidence: No Jinja sandbox or escaping is applied before the render_template_string call.

dataflow.summary: POST /sayhi name -> string interpolation into template -> render_template_string.

reachability.summary: /sayhi accepts unauthenticated GET and POST requests.

prerequisites: The attacker can submit name content containing Jinja syntax.

Finding.impact: Server-side template injection can expose application internals and may lead to code execution depending on reachable Jinja objects and runtime configuration.
Finding.remediation: Render a fixed template and pass user data as a variable. Rely on template escaping for output, and avoid render_template_string with user-controlled template source.

Finding.title: Category query parameter is concatenated into SQL

codeEvidence.label: Query parameter is formatted into WHERE clause
codeEvidence.code:
category = request.args.get(param)
...
if category:
        where = " WHERE {} = '{}'".format(param, category)
...
cursor.execute(query_build('SELECT * from public_stuff{}'.format(where)))
codeEvidence.explanation: The category query parameter is inserted into SQL with string formatting and executed by the database cursor.

codeEvidence.label: Non-Oracle queries receive statement terminator
codeEvidence.code: query_build = lambda x: x if args.database_type == 'oracle' else x + ';'
codeEvidence.explanation: The query builder appends a semicolon for most database types, reinforcing that raw SQL strings are built and submitted.

rootCause.summary: The route builds SQL with string interpolation instead of parameterized queries.

validation.summary: Static validation confirmed the category query parameter reaches cursor.execute as part of a SQL string. No database payload was executed.
validation.counterevidence: The base query targets public_stuff, but the user-controlled category value is not bound as a parameter.

dataflow.summary: GET /listservices category -> WHERE string -> SELECT string -> cursor.execute.

reachability.summary: /listservices is a GET route and does not require authentication.

prerequisites: The database backend accepts attacker-controlled SQL syntax in the constructed statement.
The configured database account has access to data or operations of interest.

Finding.impact: An attacker may alter query semantics, read unintended table data such as seeded secret_stuff rows, trigger errors, or affect database state depending on backend and privileges.
Finding.remediation: Use parameterized queries for category filtering and avoid constructing SQL from request parameters.

Finding.title: JWT verifier accepts None and HS256 algorithms based on untrusted token header

codeEvidence.label: Verifier allows RS256, HS256, and None
codeEvidence.explanation: The accepted algorithm list includes unsigned None tokens and symmetric HS256 in addition to RS256.

codeEvidence.label: Verification dispatches from unverified header
codeEvidence.explanation: The token's untrusted alg header selects the verification implementation.

codeEvidence.label: None branch accepts empty signature
codeEvidence.explanation: The None branch returns claims from an unsigned token when the signature segment is empty and claims pass basic checks.

codeEvidence.label: User page trusts sub claim for admin state and exposes JWKS
codeEvidence.explanation: The route uses the verified sub claim to determine admin display state and publishes public key material through JWKS.

rootCause.summary: JWT verification trusts the token header to select the verification algorithm and includes insecure None and HS256 branches.

validation.summary: Static validation confirmed accepted None/HS256 branches and admin-state dependence on token claims. No forged token was submitted.
validation.counterevidence: The manual branches do check issuer, audience, and time claims, but those values are attacker-controllable inside an unsigned or attacker-signed token candidate.

dataflow.summary: Cookie authentication token -> verify_token -> unverified alg header dispatch -> claims -> sub == admin check.

reachability.summary: /user reads the authentication cookie if present; /user/jwks is exposed as GET.

prerequisites: The attacker can set an authentication cookie.
The attacker can construct claims satisfying issuer, audience, nbf, iat, and exp checks.

Finding.impact: An attacker can potentially forge an admin subject claim, bypassing the intended guest identity and any future admin-gated behavior built on this check.
Finding.remediation: Pin verification to a single expected algorithm for the key type, reject None, do not use public RSA key bytes as an HMAC secret, and avoid dispatching verification behavior from untrusted token headers.

coverageLimitations: No runtime exploit requests were sent.
No external database backend was selected or tested.
Dependency advisories were not checked against exact installed versions because no lockfile or environment inventory is present.
